title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Besides a feeling of distance from everyone, Natasha felt a particular estrangement from the members of her own family. All of them—her father, mother, and Sonya—were so near, so familiar, so ordinary, that all their words and feelings seemed an insult to the world in which she had been living lately. She felt not merely indifferent toward them but actively hostile. She heard Dunyasha's words about Pyotr Ilyich and a misfortune but did not take them in.
"What misfortune? What misfortune can happen to them? They just live their old, quiet, ordinary life," thought Natasha.

As she entered the ballroom, her father was hurrying out of her mother's room. His face was crumpled and wet with tears. He had obviously rushed out to give vent to the sobs that were choking him. When he saw Natasha, he waved his arms in despair and burst into convulsive, agonized sobs that distorted his soft, round face.
"Pe... Petya... Go, go, she... is calling..." And weeping like a child and shuffling quickly on his feeble legs to a chair, he almost collapsed into it, covering his face with his hands.

Something like an electric shock seemed to run through Natasha's entire being. A terrible anguish struck her heart; she felt a dreadful tearing inside her, as if she were dying. But the pain was immediately followed by a sense of release from the oppressive weight that had prevented her from taking part in life. The sight of her father, the terribly wild cries of her mother that she heard through the door, made her instantly forget herself and her own grief.

She ran to her father, but he weakly waved his arm, pointing toward her mother's door. Princess Mary, pale and with trembling chin, came out of that room and, taking Natasha by the arm, said something to her. Natasha neither saw nor heard her. She went in with rapid steps, pausing for an instant at the door as if struggling with herself, then ran to her mother.
The countess was lying in an armchair in a strange and awkward position, stretching out and beating her head against the wall. Sonya and the maids were holding her arms.

"Natasha! Natasha!..." cried the countess. "It's not true... it's not true... He's lying... Natasha!" she shrieked, pushing everyone away. "Go away, all of you! It's not true! Killed!... Ha, ha, ha!... It's not true!"
Natasha put one knee on the armchair, bent over her mother, and with unexpected strength lifted her, turned her face toward herself, and held her tight.
"Mama!... Darling!... I'm here, my dearest Mama," she kept whispering without pause.
She didn't let go of her mother but struggled tenderly with her, called for a pillow and hot water, unfastened and tore open her mother's dress.
"My dearest darling... Mama, my precious!..." she whispered incessantly, kissing her head, her hands, her face, feeling her own unstoppable, streaming tears tickle her nose and cheeks.

The countess pressed her daughter's hand, closed her eyes, and became still for a moment. Suddenly she sat up with unaccustomed swiftness, glanced around vacantly, and seeing Natasha began to press her daughter's head with all her strength. Then she turned toward her daughter's face, which was wincing with pain, and gazed at it for a long time.
"Natasha, you love me?" she said in a soft, trusting whisper. "Natasha, you wouldn't deceive me? You'll tell me the whole truth?"
Natasha looked at her with eyes full of tears, and in her look there was nothing but love and a plea for forgiveness.
"My darling Mama!" she repeated, straining every power of her love to find some way of taking upon herself the crushing weight of grief that was destroying her mother.

And again, in a futile struggle with reality, her mother—refusing to believe she could go on living when her beloved boy had been killed in the prime of life—escaped from reality into a world of delirium.

Natasha did not remember how that day passed, nor the night, nor the following day and night. She did not sleep and did not leave her mother's side. Her tireless, patient love seemed to completely surround the countess at every moment—not explaining or consoling, but simply calling her back to life.

During the third night, the countess was quiet for a few minutes, and Natasha rested her head on the arm of her chair and closed her eyes, but opened them again when she heard the bedstead creak. The countess was sitting up in bed and speaking softly.
"How glad I am you've come. You're tired. Won't you have some tea?" Natasha went up to her. "You've gotten prettier and more grown-up," continued the countess, taking her daughter's hand.
"Mama! What are you saying..."
"Natasha, he is no more, no more!"
And embracing her daughter, the countess began to weep for the first time.
